vignette:
Viktor Hale is a 56-year-old married musician of European descent who presents with a PCL-5 score of 71 following a sexual assault that occurred approximately eighteen months ago. He was assaulted by a male authority figure - a well-established producer who had invited him to a private studio session under professional pretenses. The assault took place in a confined space, and Viktor recalls with terrible clarity the man's physical weight, the sight of blood from where his hand struck a surface, and the overwhelming presence of a particular cologne - heavy, cedar-based - that the producer wore. What he cannot reconstruct is the sequence of events that connected those fragments: there are stretches of the encounter that remain entirely blank to him, and he has never been able to tell himself a coherent story of what happened that night. He knows what he knows in pieces, and the pieces do not form a whole.

In the months that followed, Viktor found that certain sensory moments could collapse the distance between then and now without warning. The sight of any physical altercation - even a shove between strangers on the street - would drop him immediately into a state of raw vigilance. Blood, encountered during a minor kitchen accident or glimpsed on a television screen, produced the same effect. Most destabilising of all was scent: on one occasion a fellow musician at a rehearsal wore a cologne with a similar cedar note, and Viktor left the room without explanation and did not return. These triggers fed directly into a sustained state of threat - his nervous system, already primed, would escalate rapidly into irritability, angry outbursts that frightened him as much as those around him, and a hypervigilance to sudden movements by others that made ensemble playing feel genuinely dangerous.

The fragmented, incoherent quality of his memory has become one of the central engines of his distress. Because he cannot narrate what happened - even privately, even to himself - he cannot locate the danger in the past. The memory exists not as a story with a beginning and an end but as a set of live sensory charges, and this means that his triggers carry the full weight of the original threat rather than the weight of something remembered. The incompleteness of the memory also drives the threat appraisal directly: Viktor is certain, in a way he cannot fully articulate, that what he cannot remember is worse than what he can, and this certainty keeps his body in a permanent state of preparation for something unspecified and therefore inescapable.

In response to this sustained threat, Viktor began organising his life around containment. He identified the places where he felt safe - his home studio, the back garden, one particular corner of a café two blocks from his house - and he has not meaningfully left that geography in months. He stopped attending the open sessions and informal gatherings that had been the social fabric of his professional life, avoiding the musicians, producers, and industry contacts he had known before the assault. He has never allowed himself to feel or express anger, suppressing it the moment it rises, convinced that if he lets it surface he will become something he cannot control. He avoids any situation involving authority figures - managers, venue owners, anyone in a position of institutional power - which has effectively ended his ability to negotiate his own career. His wife has noticed that he is no longer the person she married, and the distance between them has grown in proportion to the territory he has ceded to avoidance.

What is particularly insidious is the way his strategies have closed off the possibility of resolution. By pushing the memory away each time it begins to surface before it can complete itself, Viktor ensures that the fragments remain raw and unprocessed. The suppression of anger and the avoidance of social contact mean that he never encounters the triggers in a context that might allow them to lose their charge; instead, when they do break through - a sudden movement in his peripheral vision, a scent on the air - they arrive with full force and confirm his belief that nowhere, and no one, is safe.

What finally brought Viktor to seek help was a session he had been trying to complete for weeks: a recording he had promised a close friend, done in his own home studio, that he has been unable to finish because he cannot remain in the room long enough. He is most afraid that whatever he cannot remember will eventually surface and destroy him. What he is hoping for, more quietly, is that someone might help him find a way to carry this that does not require surrendering everything he has built.
